question: Can a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-style learned row operator replace fixed softmax in vision-transformer self-attention and improve accuracy, transfer, generalization, or interpretability enough to justify its added parameters and compute?

key_findings.claim: Fourier-KArAt turns each query-key score row into learned, generally signed mixing weights by applying a Fourier KAN from N token scores to a rank-r latent vector and a linear projection back to N tokens.
key_findings.evidence: The full N-by-N KAN operator is reported as infeasible, so the main architecture uses r=12, Fourier grid G, and either separate head/layer operators (blockwise) or one operator per head shared across all layers (universal). The probability-simplex projection is optional and omitted in the main experiments because it sharply reduces accuracy.

anchors.section: 3 How Can We Design Learnable Attention? and Equation 1

key_findings.claim: The accuracy benefit is confined mainly to small ViTs on CIFAR; every KArAt model loses to its paired baseline on ImageNet-1K, and most Small/Base comparisons also lose.
key_findings.evidence: ViT-Tiny improves from 72.76 to 76.69 on CIFAR-10 and from 43.53 to 46.75 on CIFAR-100, but its ImageNet-1K variants score 59.11 and 57.97 versus 59.15. ViT-Small KArAt reaches 54.11/53.86 versus 53.47 on CIFAR-100 but loses on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; every ViT-Base variant loses on all three datasets. Thus the abstract's broad 'outperform or comparable' wording hides a strong model- and dataset-size interaction.

key_findings.claim: The paper's transfer claim is not supported as a performance gain: all 18 KArAt fine-tuning cells are below their corresponding vanilla ViT values.
key_findings.evidence: Across ViT-Tiny, Small, and Base, both blockwise and universal KArAt variants lose on SVHN, Flowers-102, and STL-10. For example, ViT-Base reports 97.74/92.24/97.26 while G1B reports 96.83/89.66/95.30. These may be modest losses in some cells, but they contradict the prose inference that the method 'transfers well' unless that phrase is defined only as retaining high absolute accuracy.

key_findings.claim: Generalization beyond the base classifier is consistently worse overall, including large drops on Swin and ViT-Det that are not a 'small performance gap.'
key_findings.evidence: ConViT-Tiny improves on CIFAR-10 from 71.36 to 75.57 but drops on ImageNet-1K from 57.91 to 56.57; Swin-Tiny drops from 84.83 to 79.34 on CIFAR-10 and from 76.14 to 73.19 on ImageNet. With ImageNet-pretrained ViT-Det, vanilla box/mask AP is 32.34/28.35 versus 22.48/20.11 for G1B and 26.68/24.01 for G1U; all random-initialization KArAt results are also lower.

key_findings.claim: Attention transfer gives one intriguing positive result for Tiny models, but it does not establish that the visualized pre-activation maps are explanatory or that KArAt itself is the better architecture.
key_findings.evidence: A vanilla ViT-Tiny trained using frozen maps from ViT-Tiny+G3B reaches 77.94/48.91 on CIFAR-10/100, exceeding both vanilla Tiny (72.76/43.53) and KArAt Tiny (76.69/46.29). The analogous Base transfers fail. Separately, the paper admits KArAt outputs are not probabilities and visualizes pre-KArAt query-key scores after deleting negative values; those scores precede the learned operator, so the pictures cannot directly demonstrate that the operator yields more interpretable mixing weights.

key_findings.claim: KArAt's modest parameter overhead conceals much larger activation cost, memory use, and training time.
key_findings.evidence: At r=12, training memory rises from 7.44 to 17.36/16.97 GB for Base, 4.15 to 11.73/11.21 GB for Small, and 2.94 to 7.48/7.29 GB for Tiny. Attention-activation GFLOPs rise from 0.016 to 0.268 for Base and from 0.005 to 0.168 for Tiny; Figure 7 shows substantially longer training and generally lower or model-dependent throughput. Grid size must be tuned per model, and some settings collapse.

anchors.section: C.3 Computation Time, FLOPs, Memory Requirement, and Throughput

key_findings.claim: The approximation and convergence discussion motivates Fourier features but does not prove that finite Fourier-KArAt approximates row-softmax well, trains reliably, or generalizes.
key_findings.evidence: Carleson's theorem concerns pointwise convergence of scalar periodic Fourier series as the truncation grows; KArAt instead applies a finite learned multivariate row operator to unbounded query-key scores and then projects through a rank bottleneck. The loss-landscape and weight-histogram plots are descriptive. In particular, approximately stable marginal weight histograms do not establish the invariant-measure conditions needed to guarantee optimization convergence.

method.core_idea: Replace the fixed row-wise softmax over query-key scores with a trainable KAN operator so every attention head can learn its own score-to-mixing transformation.
method.mechanism: Each score row in R^N is passed through r Fourier-KAN output units whose sin/cos coefficients are learned, then through a bias-free linear r-to-N projector. Blockwise KArAt instantiates this module for every head and layer; universal KArAt shares one module per head across layers. The resulting signed, unnormalized N-vector multiplies the value matrix directly. An optional Euclidean probability-simplex projection is evaluated but removed from the main method.
assumptions: The number of tokens N is fixed at construction time; changing image resolution, sequence length, or attention geometry requires changing learned operator dimensions.
A rank-r bottleneck inferred from a very small spectral sample preserves the token interactions needed by the learned activation.
A truncated Fourier basis is an effective parameterization on the empirical range of query-key scores even though the cited convergence theorem is asymptotic and periodic.
Signed, non-normalized KArAt outputs remain stable when used directly as value-mixing weights.
Per-model and per-dataset grid selection is available; the paper finds no universal G.

techniques.role: Learns univariate functions on every input-output edge of the score-row transformation instead of applying fixed softmax.
Parameterizes each learned unit with trainable sine and cosine coefficients over G frequencies.
Maps N scores to r=12 learned features and linearly expands them back to N to make full KArAt trainable.
Trades parameters for diversity by choosing per-layer operators or per-head operators shared across all layers.
Tests whether restoring positivity and unit-sum constraints helps; the reported collapse motivates signed unnormalized weights.
Freezes attention matrices from a trained KArAt model while retraining a vanilla value branch to test whether the matrices carry reusable signal.
Uses singular-value plots as a heuristic for selecting the latent rank and comparing score-matrix structure.

evaluations.setting: ViT-Tiny, Small, and Base trained for 100 epochs on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K with separately selected Fourier grids.
evaluations.metric: Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy, parameters, training curves.
evaluations.result: Tiny gains up to 3.93 Top-1 points on CIFAR-10 and 3.22 on CIFAR-100, but KArAt loses in all six ImageNet variant comparisons and in most Small/Base comparisons.
evaluations.baseline: Matched softmax ViTs trained with the paper's recipe.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet-pretrained ViT variants fine-tuned on SVHN, Flowers-102, and STL-10.
evaluations.result: Every one of the 18 KArAt cells is lower than its paired vanilla model, with losses ranging from small fractions of a point to about 2.8 points.
evaluations.baseline: Corresponding ImageNet-pretrained vanilla ViT-Tiny, Small, or Base.

evaluations.setting: KArAt inserted into ConViT-Tiny and Swin-Tiny on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1K.
evaluations.result: ConViT gains on CIFAR-10 but loses on ImageNet; Swin loses substantially on both datasets.
evaluations.baseline: Original softmax ConViT-Tiny and Swin-Tiny under the reported recipe.

evaluations.setting: ViT-Det-Base with Mask R-CNN/FPN on MS COCO, from ImageNet-pretrained and random initialization.
evaluations.metric: Box and mask AP, AP50, and AP75.
evaluations.result: All KArAt variants lose; with pretrained initialization, the best KArAt box/mask AP is 26.68/24.01 versus 32.34/28.35, and G1B falls to 22.48/20.11.

evaluations.setting: Attention transfer from trained Tiny/Base KArAt models into newly trained vanilla ViTs on CIFAR-10/100.
evaluations.result: Tiny KArAt maps improve a vanilla Tiny beyond both source and baseline, but maps involving Base do not improve the Base baseline.
evaluations.baseline: Vanilla and KArAt models trained without transferred attention matrices.

evaluations.setting: Grid, rank, basis, base activation, operator order, hybrid-head, learning-rate, and simplex-projection ablations.
evaluations.metric: Top-1 accuracy, stability, parameters, GFLOPs, memory, time, and throughput.
evaluations.result: Performance is highly configuration-sensitive: Base G11 collapses to 50.47/40.74 on CIFAR-10; Morlet Base reaches 24.19 on CIFAR-10; simplex projection reduces Tiny G3B from 76.69 to 41.99 and Base G3B from 80.09 to 47.44. Lower r can retain accuracy but does not remove the main training overhead.
evaluations.baseline: Best main KArAt configuration and matched softmax ViT.

limitations: Author-stated: full KArAt is prohibitively expensive, while the modular version still uses about 2.5-3 times the training memory and much longer training than softmax ViTs.
Author-stated: the operator is tied to a fixed token count; varying sequences and cross-attention need major architectural modifications.
Author-stated: training becomes unstable as models grow, optimal grid size is model-specific, and compute limits prevented broader large-scale pretraining.
Reviewer inference: best-grid reporting after a wide sweep creates selection bias, while tables provide single point estimates without seed dispersion or a held-out model-selection protocol.

Reviewer inference: every transfer cell and every ViT-Det comparison is worse than baseline, so 'transfers well,' 'generalizes well,' and 'small performance gap' are materially stronger than the tables support.
Reviewer inference: pre-KArAt score visualizations cannot validate interpretability of the learned post-score operator, particularly after negative entries are discarded for display.
Reviewer inference: the Fourier and KAN representation results are motivation, not an approximation, optimization, scaling, or generalization guarantee for this finite architecture.

Reviewer inference from the official code: the release covers the core ViT classifier but omits the ConViT, Swin, ViT-Det, attention-transfer, landscape, spectral, checkpoint, and result-generation pipelines needed to reproduce much of the paper.

Reviewer inference from the official code: the advertised --basis_not_trainable option leaves Fourier coefficients trainable and freezes only their scale; the repository has no tests or continuous integration to catch this behavior.

Specification audit: Algorithm 1 omits the positivity predicate in the definition of rho, Algorithm 2 concatenates heads through N rather than h, the prose says ADAM while all hyperparameter tables and code default to AdamW, and Table 16 prints 58.07 rather than 83.45 for ViT-Base CIFAR-10.
failure_modes: Changing input resolution or sequence length produces an N mismatch between score rows and the learned KAN/linear layers.
Larger models or unsuitable grids enter sharp, unstable regimes and can lose many accuracy points or exhibit gradient explosion.
Hierarchical/windowed attention and detection pipelines lose more than plain Tiny ViTs because their interaction structure differs from the fixed global-row operator.
Restoring probability-simplex constraints collapses the tested models, while omitting them permits negative and unbounded value mixing with no probabilistic interpretation.
Selecting r from five images and three heads can miss ranks or interaction modes needed in other layers, datasets, or architectures.
A qualitative whole-object heatmap can be produced by clipping pre-activation scores even when the learned KArAt output is unstable, worse-performing, or non-explanatory.
The method can look competitive against short-schedule, low-accuracy ViT baselines yet fail to retain that relation under stronger recipes or scaling.
reusable_insights: When replacing attention normalization, report both the new operator's actual output and the pre-activation query-key scores; do not use one as evidence about the other.
A learned attention transform should be compared with cheap fixed alternatives and low-dimensional adaptive normalizers before attributing gains to a high-capacity KAN.
Evaluate every model size and downstream task as a matrix, then summarize wins, ties, and losses rather than selecting the best cells.
Treat probability-simplex projection as an architectural intervention: its catastrophic ablation here shows that signed value mixing, not merely a learned approximation to softmax, drives the method.
If sequence length enters parameter shapes, validation must include resolution/length extrapolation or explicitly scope the model to fixed-token tasks.

Small-model gains that reverse at larger scale should trigger scaling-law experiments over compute-matched baselines, multiple seeds, and jointly tuned capacity rather than post-hoc loss-landscape narratives.
A frozen learned mixing matrix can be more useful than the architecture that produced it; distillation or low-cost attention supervision may retain the signal without the expensive operator.
open_questions: Do Tiny-model gains persist against compute-matched ReLU, sigmoid, learned-entmax, polynomial, and small-MLP row transforms under a common modern ViT recipe?
Can KArAt be reformulated as a length-agnostic elementwise or kernel operator while preserving its claimed adaptability?
Which property causes the gains: Fourier periodicity, learned signed mixing, cross-token row coupling, rank restriction, or extra parameters?
Can attention-transfer improvements be reproduced across seeds and stronger baselines, and which exact pre- or post-activation matrices were transferred?
Does a KArAt output correlate with causal token importance under deletion, counterfactual, or attention-intervention tests rather than heatmap appearance?
What scaling relationship between rank, grid size, token count, heads, data, and model width predicts stable training before a full run?
Can hardware-aware grouped or separable KAN operators close the 17-34 times attention-activation FLOP gap without losing accuracy?
Would distilling KArAt attention into softmax, sigmoid, or a low-degree polynomial yield the Tiny gains at ordinary inference cost?

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: KAN places learned univariate spline functions on network edges and motivates KArAt's operator parameterization. KArAt applies this idea specifically to entire self-attention score rows and substitutes Fourier bases plus a rank bottleneck.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN or MLP: A Fairer Comparison
competitive_landscape.difference: Yu et al. control parameters and FLOPs and find MLPs generally outperform KANs outside symbolic representation. It motivates a missing compute-matched MLP row-operator baseline for determining whether KArAt gains come from KAN structure rather than extra capacity.

competitive_landscape.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Transformer
competitive_landscape.difference: KAT replaces channel-mixing MLPs with rational Group-KAN layers, uses weight sharing, CUDA kernels, and variance-preserving initialization, and reports ImageNet scaling. KArAt leaves the MLP intact and instead learns the attention score transform, with much worse memory scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: KAA: Kolmogorov-Arnold Attention for Enhancing Attentive Graph Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: KAA predates KArAt's arXiv submission and inserts a KAN into graph neighbor-pair scoring, then normalizes the scores for GNN aggregation. KArAt instead maps a complete ViT score row to a new complete row, so its narrow MHSA construction remains distinct but the broad name and 'first learnable attention' framing do not.

competitive_landscape.title: Adaptively Sparse Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Adaptive entmax learns a shape/sparsity parameter for each attention head, replacing fixed softmax with a trainable differentiable normalizer while retaining probability semantics. It is far less expressive than KArAt but directly refutes an unqualified claim that attention activation had not previously been learned.

competitive_landscape.title: Synthesizer: Rethinking Self-Attention in Transformer Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Synthesizer directly learns synthetic attention weights, including factorized variants, without query-key token interactions. KArAt retains query-key scores and learns their row transformation, but it is not the first Transformer mechanism to learn attention weights with an auxiliary network.

competitive_landscape.title: Escaping the Gradient Vanishing: Periodic Alternatives of Softmax in Attention Mechanism
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. replace the exponential in attention normalization with periodic functions and test a LeViT-style vision model. Their functions are hand-designed rather than a general learned KAN row operator, but the paper is a close uncited predecessor to Fourier-based alternatives for vision attention.

competitive_landscape.title: Replacing softmax with ReLU in Vision Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: ReLU attention divided by sequence length approaches or matches softmax scaling from small to large ImageNet-21k ViTs without a learned N-to-N operator. It is the essential efficiency and scaling baseline absent from KArAt's experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: Theory, Analysis, and Best Practices for Sigmoid Self-Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Properly normalized sigmoid attention matches softmax across language, vision, and speech at scale, has a universality/regularity analysis, and a hardware-aware kernel reported faster than FlashAttention2. KArAt is more expressive per row but fixed-length and dramatically heavier.

competitive_landscape.title: Rethinking Attention: Polynomial Alternatives to Softmax in Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: This work argues attention stability comes from Frobenius-norm regularization and uses simple polynomials that need not be positive, normalized, or sparse. It offers a theory-driven signed alternative and a much cheaper control for KArAt's claim that basis-learned flexibility is necessary.

competitive_landscape.title: Vision KAN: Towards an Attention-Free Backbone for Vision with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: ViK replaces pairwise attention with patch-wise RBF-KAN transforms, separable local mixing, and a low-rank global map, reporting ImageNet-1K performance at linear complexity. It directly targets KArAt's fixed-length, quadratic, and memory-heavy failure modes rather than learning the softmax replacement.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first learnable attention for ViTs, a general KAN operator that can use arbitrary bases, and the first demonstration that attention itself can be learned.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Its concrete construction is a per-head KAN mapping from an entire query-key score row through a low-rank latent space back to a full row, evaluated with Fourier, wavelet, rational, and base-function variants.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is narrower: this appears to be the first basis-general KAN row operator used in place of ViT softmax with blockwise/universal sharing and a broad diagnostic suite. Learned attention weights, learned normalizer shape, periodic attention alternatives, and KAN-based attention scoring all predate it. Empirically, the contribution is a revealing pilot and negative scaling study more than evidence that learned KAN attention is generally better.

reviewer_notes: Read all 32 pages of arXiv v3 and audited all 13 figures, 20 tables, two algorithms, displayed derivations, appendix ablations, and references. The arXiv source package was inspected in full: main TeX/bibliography/style files plus all 27 figure assets. Every visual page was rendered and checked, including small labels in the compute, landscape, spectral, detection, and attention panels. The official repository was audited at commit a193a159d68369d63ad2e641ef4693e21c3e3fed (13 commits; last change 2025-07-08): all 15 Python modules compile, and a lightweight Fourier MultiKAN forward/backward check confirms the advertised freeze flag does not freeze Fourier coefficients. No end-to-end training was attempted because the release requires GPU-scale datasets and its pinned timm/einops/fvcore environment was not installed. The repository has no tests, CI, checkpoints, logs, or code for most secondary experiments. Eleven primary arXiv/OpenReview competitors were checked through 2026-08-23. Material contradictions are the universal transfer/generalization prose versus uniformly worse transfer and detection tables, interpretability claims based on pre-operator maps, overbroad priority language, and theory/convergence language stronger than the cited results support.
